name: Sachse
seo_title: Christmas Events for Kids in Sachse, TX 2026
seo_description: Kids' Christmas in Sachse, TX: the Christmas Extravaganza lighted parade and tree lighting on December 2, with Santa, a snow slide and hayrides.
lede: The story of Christmas in Sachse starts with a railroad deal in 1886, when William Sachse gave the railroad 100 feet of right of way and it built a depot and named the town for him. Today the town's big holiday night is the Christmas Extravaganza, a lighted parade down Miles Road followed by a tree lighting, a snow slide, a petting zoo, hayrides and Santa.
sections: The Christmas Extravaganza on Miles Road

The City of Sachse holds its Christmas Extravaganza on Wednesday, December 2, 2026. The lighted Christmas parade starts at 6 pm on Miles Road, and the city says spectators may sit along the road to watch. Miles Road is closed to traffic from Sachse Road to Haverhill Lane between 5:50 and 7 pm. At 7 pm the city lights a tree in front of the Michael J. Felix Community Center at the Sachse City Complex, 3815 Sachse Road, and activities follow, including a snow slide, a petting zoo, hayrides, games and visits with Santa. The city's calendar lists the event as free. Questions go to the parks department at 469 429 0275.
How a deal with the railroad named the town

Sachse is named for William C. Sachse, a native of Prussia, and his wife Elizabeth Straly Sachse, who received a 320 acre Peters colony land grant in 1846, according to the Handbook of Texas. The Gulf, Colorado and Santa Fe Railway came through in 1886. The city's own history says Sachse gave the railroad 100 feet of right of way across his land and, in exchange, the railroad built a depot and named the town Sachse. The post office had been registered as Saxie until the name changed to Sachse in 1892. Sachse was incorporated in April 1956 with about 250 people.
Cotton, onions and the train that Mr. Sachse watched

By the late 1920s Sachse had a business district with the train depot, two onion sheds, cattle pens, two gins, two general stores and a bank, according to the city's history, and onions competed with cotton as a major cash crop. The Sachse Historical Society museum keeps that story. Its copper roof house, built in the 1890s on Railroad Street with gingerbread trim and a wrought iron fence, is where William Sachse spent his last years watching the trains go by. For light rail, DART opened its Blue Line extension from Downtown Garland Station to Downtown Rowlett Station on December 3, 2012.
